6.250.m: Śrī Rudra said: / Pradyumna was born to Kṛṣṇa by Rukmiṇī from a portion of Madana.
Born of Madana and possessing great strength, he slew Śambara.
To him, from the daughter of Rukmin, was born Aniruddha.

He too married Bāṇa's daughter, the maiden named Uṣā.

She, having properly enjoyed in a dream for sixteen years him who was dark like the petal of a blue lotus, whose eyes resembled white lotuses, who had long arms and was adorned with wondrous ornaments, woke up and, not seeing him before her,
tormented by love, her mind bewildered, she wailed in many ways: "Having abandoned me, O youthful one with a face like a red lotus, where are you, where have you gone?"
Then her friend, a girl named Citralekhā, seeing her reduced to such a state, asked: "For what reason is your mind bewildered?"
She too related duly the husband she had obtained in her dream.
Then she, having drawn the best of all gods, humans, and others on a canvas, showed it to her.
She also properly presented those born in the Yadu lineage: Kṛṣṇa, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and the others.

Considering Kṛṣṇa among them, and then Pradyumna, upon seeing Aniruddha she embraced [the picture], saying, "It is he! It is he!"

Then Citralekhā, having gone to Dvāravatī together with many illusion-wielding Daitya women, [found] sleeping at night in the inner quarters

quarters adorned with shrines, palaces, and the like, she placed [him] upon the bed of that daughter of Bāṇa.

He too, having awakened, seeing Uṣā in the delightful fire of Cupid—endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with varied ornaments,
and garlands, golden-complexioned, with beautiful hair and shapely breasts—embraced her tightly, and, like a scent-elephant with a female elephant, enjoyed her at pleasure, filled with great delight.
In this manner, as he was sporting uninterruptedly for a month, the elder Daitya women dwelling in the inner quarters discovered Aniruddha and reported it to the king.
The king, his eyes copper-red with rage, filled with great astonishment, dispatched attendants before him, saying, "Bring him here!"
They too quickly ascended the royal palace and came to seize Aniruddha who was resting on the princess's bed.
Seeing them advancing, he playfully uprooted a pillar of the palace and within a mere muhūrta crushed a hundred thousand attendants with that pillar alone.

Then the lord of the Daityas, seeing the attendants slain, was astonished; and told by the divine sage that "he is Śrī Kṛṣṇa's grandson," he took up his bow and came in person near him to seize Aniruddha.
Aniruddha, seeing that thousand-armed king coming to fight, whirled an iron club and hurled it at Bāṇa.
[Bāṇa] severed that club with an arrow shot from his bow.
Then, binding Aniruddha tightly with a serpent-missile, he placed him in his inner quarters.
Now Kṛṣṇa, having learned of these events through the divine sage, set out together with Baladeva and Pradyumna and his army, mounted upon the king of birds, to cut down the forest of Bāṇa's arms.

Formerly, Śaṅkara had been worshiped by Bali's son; being pleased, he said, "Choose a boon!"

Bāṇa asked this boon of the Lord: "Sit always at the gate of my city to protect it, and destroy the enemy army that arrives."

seeing Vāsudeva arrive with his army, he mounted his bull, equipped with all weapons and surrounded by his sons and attendants, and marched out to fight.

Kṛṣṇa too, seeing that lord of spirits clad in an elephant hide, bearing a skull and ashes, wearing blazing serpents as ornaments, tawny, three-eyed, holding a trident,

the destroyer of Tripura—having stationed his army far behind, accompanied by Balabhadra and Pradyumna, began to fight with Rudra
First there took place a dreadful battle between Kṛṣṇa and Śaṅkara, / with arrows resembling the fires of cosmic destruction released from the Pināka and Śārṅga bows.
Rāma fought with Bāṇa, and Pradyumna with the six-faced one; / the two pairs fought with great valor, like lions vehement in strength.
Vināyaka struck the Yādava on the chest with his tusk; / Rāma, taking up his pestle, struck his tusk.
With his tusk split, the rat-riding deity fled in haste; / from that time on in this world, the lord of gaṇas, his tusk broken,
has been called Ekadanta by gods, Dānavas, and Gandharvas. / The peacock-riding god fought together with Pradyumna.
He whose weapon is the plow routed the gaṇas with his pestle. / Having fought for a very long time with Kṛṣṇa, that blue-and-red god,
setting the intensely blazing fever of burning heat upon an arrow, / furiously loosed it then, his eyes deeply reddened.
Kṛṣṇa warded off that missile with the fever of shivering cold. / Discharged by those two, Hari and Hara, these two fevers
entered the human world in great force by the command of those two alone. / Whatever people listen to this battle between Hari and Śaṅkara,
they all, freed from fever, attain health. / Then Hṛṣīkeśa, the slayer of Madhu,
fixing upon an arrow the irresistible missile of delusion, loosed it at the lord of spirits. / Enchanted by that weapon, he repeatedly yawned.
Śaṅkara, the lord of the thirty gods, fell fainting to the ground. / Seeing his father deluded, the valiant six-faced deity,
riding a peacock and raising his spear, rushed forward to fight Kṛṣṇa. / With a mere roar, Kṛṣṇa turned him back right there.
Having thus conquered the three-eyed trident-bearer, the glorious best of Yadus / blew his loud-sounding conch, Pāñcajanya.
Hearing that Śaṅkara together with his sons had then been conquered by Kṛṣṇa, / Bāṇa mounted his chariot and went to fight Keśava.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa suddenly, mounted on Garuḍa, / he covered Govinda with abundant showers of weapons and missiles:
with maces, iron clubs, spears, pikes, and javelins, / with slings, swords, discs, and arrows incessantly.
Janārdana severed them all with his discus alone; / he dispatched the Sudarśana to cut off his arms.
The thousand-spoked Sudarśana, hurled at the king of Dānavas, / swiftly cut the forest of his arms into a thousand pieces.
At this moment, O goddess, Pārvatī of strict vows / approached Hari and spoke with folded hands.
Pārvatī said: / "O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the Universe, Nārāyaṇa, ocean of compassion! / O Lord of gods, best of Yadus, I was your handmaiden in a previous existence.
"A boon was granted by you to me then on Mount Kauśala, / everlasting marital bliss, O gentle one, pleased as a great-souled one."
"Foremost among the thousand of your names, O pervasive lord, / is celebrated by the sages: 'Giver of marital bliss to Gaurī'."
"Make that true, O Govinda, eternal one mounted on Garuḍa! / Therefore, O god, you ought to bring my husband back to life!"
Rudra said: / Addressed thus then by the goddess, lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa / withdrew the weapon by which her husband had been stupefied.
Completely freed from Kṛṣṇa's weapon, Śiva, lord of all beings, / arose, and with folded hands praised the lord of the worlds.
Śaṅkara said: / "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, lord of the universe, Blessed One, Supreme Person, / supreme sovereign, supreme lord, without beginning or end, imperishable!
[Your] intense power among human beings consists of taking on a body; / this movement of yours is everything, the very mark of your measure.
Be gracious to me, homage to you! Be gracious to me, eternal one! / Be gracious to me, master of the universe! Be gracious, Acyuta, Keśava!
You alone are the creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the worlds, the world's teacher; / you alone are the form of conscious and unconscious matter, brahman, ruler of the gods!
You are the beginning, you are without beginning, you are the lord and Śeṣa; / you are the Great Principle, you are the supreme brahman, you indeed are the inner self!
You are the best of all immortals, you are immortal, O lord of the gods; / you are the lord of mortals, you are their origin, through your benevolence, O Lord!
Produced from your breath are both the supreme [soul] and the eternal individual souls, / and they are nurtured directly by the weight of your parental affection.
In the supreme abode of the perishable and imperishable, the hymns ever resting in the gods, / you establish yourself above the universe through the service of servitude, not otherwise.
Whoever does not know you in this world is completely deluded, creator of all; / the wise know the supreme abode, the lord of high and low, through servitude.
Attuned, they indeed dwell together with the thirty [gods] in that abode; / an ordinary man worships afar to bow perpetually to your abode.
The fourth state belongs to you, O lovely-haired one; it becomes appropriate for you. / Pairs proclaim you, O witness, eternal Yadava.
Your eternal names, actions, and qualities, / and your lordly powers, beyond qualities, these two supreme [scriptures] declare.
These former and latter revealed scriptures, whose forms consist of action and knowledge, / are the two praiseworthy young women with children praising you, O Keśava.
You are consciousness, the supreme brahman; by you who are wise, eternal one, / give life through this consciousness, by you who are the supreme self itself.
Departing from that body, through your grace alone, / one possesses knowledge of the self given by you in the supreme heaven of the afterlife.
Pure consciousness and discernment, intellect, vision, and steadfastness— / he attains all desires, and then he becomes immortal.
This cognition, the self, that which is this mind in the heart, / wisdom and comprehension, memory and intention,
austerity, acts of worship, desire, and condition: these, O Lord, / are names of consciousness, O treasure of compassion!
This you are: the supreme brahman; this you are: Prajāpati; / this you are: Indra and Rudra; this you are: all the deities.
All these beings are you alone, O supreme lord: / children, friends, the breath of life, and other things likewise, O eternal one!
Beings born from a womb, born from an egg, born from sweat, and born from shoots; / horses, cows, men, elephants, and other creatures;
whatever collection of living beings there is, both moving creatures / and stationary things, O Lord—all indeed arise from you.
For thus the revealed scriptures proclaim you, Hari, pervading all; / impelled by you alone, people act toward good and bad ends.
Therefore, whatever offense has been committed by me, O Lord, / forgive it, O ocean of mercy, through your most auspicious qualities!
“Salutations to you, lotus-eyed one, Govinda, Acyuta, Mādhava! / O Vāsudeva, praiseworthy by the world, Nārāyaṇa, salutations to you!”
I bow, master of the universe, Nṛsiṃha, compassionate one! / Lord of Śrī, all-pervading, glorious one, supreme self, homage be to you!
You whose own abode is Vaikuṇṭha, worshipped by the eternally liberated, O Lord! / Lord of the threefold Veda, homage to you, Rāma, lotus-eyed one!
To the destroyer of the earth's burden, Kṛṣṇa, whose nature is bliss, / to Viṣṇu, victorious, homage to you, delight of the Yadus!"
Having thus praised Govinda and bowed down, the husband of Umā, / the lord of beings, with folded hands, spoke these words in a deep voice.
Rudra said: / "A boon was indeed granted by me, O Lord, to this Bāṇa, son of Bali; / and I granted him a boon formerly when requested by him.
Immortality, O best of the Yadus! You are capable of doing everything; / therefore you ought to protect this son of Bali, who is dear to me."
Saying 'So be it,' the Blessed One then [looked upon] Bāṇa, the son of Bali, / who had reached danger to his life, with severed arms and covered in blood.
Withdrawing his discus, Govinda, the treasure of compassion, released him. / Having secured the release of the son of Bali, Śaṅkara of strict vows,
mounting the chief of bulls together with Pārvatī, the lord / went to Mount Kailāsa, his dwelling place.
And that Bāṇa, having paid homage to Rāma and Kṛṣṇa of great strength, / went with them to his city and released the son of Madana.
Having honored him suitably with divine garments and ornaments, / he gave Uṣā to him, the grandson of Kṛṣṇa, descendant of Śūra.
Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, having duly married that Aniruddha [to her], / were then honored there by Bāṇa together with Pradyumna.
Janārdana, having mounted Aniruddha together with Uṣā / upon a divine chariot there, then set out for Dvāravatī.
Accompanied by Rāma and Pradyumna, accompanied by his army, Hari / entered the lovely city like Maghavan with the gods.

6.250.m:
In a house made of various gems, Aniruddha, filled with joy, / made love constantly to Bāṇa's daughter with various pleasures.

Thus ends the two hundred and fiftieth chapter, named “The Account of the Battle with Bāṇāsura,” in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, the great Purāṇa in the collection of fifty-five thousand [verses].

Chapter two hundred and fifty-one.
Śrī Rudra said: “Then Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva,”

the king of Kāśī, in a solitary spot in Vārāṇasī, worshipping Maheśa for twelve years without taking food, muttered the five-syllable mantra.

At the time of completing the preliminary rites, he worshipped Śaṅkara with the lotus of his own eye.

Then the trident-bearing husband of Umā, pleased, said to him: 'Choose a boon!'

He said to the pleased, boon-granting Śiva, the five-faced lord of all beings: 'Grant me a form equal to Vāsudeva!'

Śiva [was asked] by him: 'Four-armed, furnished with conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with eyes resembling lotus petals, a crown equal to Vāsudeva's,

charming locks of hair, yellow garments, the Kaustubha ornament, and other signs—give these to me as well.' Thus petitioned, Śiva

granted him everything.

He, claiming 'I am Vāsudeva,' deluded all the worlds.

Once, Nārada, having arrived from heaven, approached that lord of Kāśī who was arrogant with the pride of his strength, and said: 'Without defeating the son of Vasudeva, there is no state of being Vāsudeva.'

6.250.m:
At that very moment, having mounted a chariot fashioned with a Garuḍa banner, he reached Dvārakā with the force of a fourfold akṣauhiṇī.

Standing in his golden vehicle at the city gate, he sent a messenger, saying: 'I, Vāsudeva, have arrived for battle. Unless you conquer me, your claim to be Vāsudeva is void.'

Hearing that, Viṣṇu mounted the son of Vinatā to fight with Pauṇḍraka; having gone forth to the city gate, he saw Pauṇḍraka seated upon a chariot with the force of an akṣauhiṇī, holding a conch, discus, mace, and lotus in his hands.

Then Kṛṣṇa took up the Śārṅga bow and, with arrows blazing like the fire of cosmic dissolution, in merely a moment burnt without remainder that great akṣauhiṇī army accompanied by horses, elephants, and foot soldiers.

With a single arrow, he playfully severed the weapons held in his hands—the conch, discus, mace, and the rest.

With the sacred Sudarśana, he severed his lotus-like head adorned with a crown and earrings, and caused it to fall into the inner apartments of Vārāṇasī.

Seeing that, all the inhabitants of Kāśī were astonished, wondering: 'What is this?'

Hearing that his father had been slain by the blessed Vāsudeva, that son of Pauṇḍraka named Daṇḍapāṇi, urged by his mother upon death and directed by his family priest, worshipped Śaṅkara with a sacrifice dedicated to Maheśvara.

Pleased, he graciously gave him a destructive spirit of Maheśvara, capable of slaying Kṛṣṇa out of his desire to kill him.

The king of Kāśī, seeing that female spirit of Maheśvara whose body was swollen with a mass of flames, whose cluster of matted hair blazed, whose eyes were tawny,

who held a trident in her hand, who was smeared with ashes as unguent, adorned with a garland of human skulls, terrifying to all the gods,

and granted by Rudra, dispatched her, saying: 'Slay Kṛṣṇa along with his sons, wives, and kinsmen!'

She, striking fear into all the worlds, burning the entire earth today with her own splendor, uttering roars like the thunderbolts of cosmic dissolution, reached Dvārakā.

Seeing her and thinking it was the great cosmic dissolution, all the people there made a clamor of distress and reported it to Kṛṣṇa.

Kṛṣṇa too said to them all, 'Do not fear!' and seeing that highly dreadful spirit standing at the gate of the rampart in such a manner, he suddenly hurled at that spirit the thousand-spoked Sudarśana, capable of warding off all weapons and missiles.

Seeing the great Sudarśana, with splendor equal to ten million suns at the end of an eon, rising a hundred leagues, endowed with every blazing missile, golden, filled with brilliance,

capable of maintaining the cosmic dissolution of the entire world, thousand-spoked, bowed to by all the gods, and the refuge of the world,

she, with her splendor destroyed and afflicted with fear, fled wailing towards Vārāṇasī.

6.250.m:
Sudarśana, too, pursued that spirit closely.

Afflicted with fear and screaming, she entered the inner apartments of that king of Kāśī.

Sudarśana too, having reached that city of Vārāṇasī, [beheaded] the son of Pauṇḍraka named Daṇḍapāṇi along with his servants, forces, and vehicles, who—

and also that female spirit of Maheśvara, being worshipped by all the gods and great sages,

re-entered Kṛṣṇa's hand in Dvāravatī, very gentle as if at the end of a cosmic age.

And on this matter these verses are sung: / Having burned by its might that army that ceased releasing weapons and missiles, / and having reduced that spirit to ashes, [it burned] then the city of Vārāṇasī,

abounding in chariots and elephants, along with horses, men, and women, / with all its treasuries and granaries, difficult even for gods to gaze upon,

with all its houses, ramparts, and courtyards marked by gateways: / Hari's discus burnt that entire city.

Having an unslackened capacity of movement, achieving what was impossible to achieve, / that discus, blazing with brilliance, returned to Viṣṇu's hand.

6.252.m: Śrī Rudra said: / Then the ruler of Magadha, hating the Yādavas after the slaying of Kaṃsa, constantly afflicted them. Suffering, they spoke to Kṛṣṇa.
And Kṛṣṇa, having summoned Bhīma and Arjuna, took counsel: / 'He has worshipped Rudra; by his favor he cannot be slain by weapons, but he must be killed by some means or other.'
Then, having deliberated, he said to Bhīma: 'Fight a wrestling duel against him.' And he agreed.
Then Vāsudeva, praiseworthy by the entire world of moving and unmoving beings, went along with Bhīma and Arjuna in the guise of Brahmins to the city of Jarāsandha and entered his inner apartment.

He too, having vanquished Kṣatriyas of great prowess in battle, captured them by force, and confined them in his dwelling, would kill them one by one every month on the dark fourteenth day and offer them with their very blood as an oblation to Bhairava.

While Jarāsaṃdha was engaged in such slaughter of the rulers of all realms, [Kṛṣṇa], rising up, entered his house in the guise of a Brahmin along with Bhīma and Arjuna.

Seeing them, Jarāsaṃdha bowed down like a staff, seated them on appropriate seats, and honored them with the madhuparka offering,
“I have accomplished my duty. For what purpose have you come to my presence? That must be stated; I shall give all of that to you,” he said.
Laughing, Vāsudeva said to that king: “We, Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma, and Arjuna, have come for battle. Choose any one of us for single combat,” he declared.
He too said, “So be it,” and then chose the son of the wind-god for single combat.

Then a terrifying wrestling match took place on both sides between Bhīma and Jarāsaṃdha continuously for twenty-five days.

Then, urged by Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vāyu split his body in two and threw it to the ground.
having slain Jarāsaṃdha through the son of Pāṇḍu, Vāsudeva also released those kings imprisoned by Jarāsaṃdha.
Having slain Jarāsaṃdha through the son of Vāyu, the descendant of Yadu / released the kings imprisoned in his house.
Having bowed to and praised Madhusūdana there, / they all went to their respective lands, protected by Kṛṣṇa.
Then, having gone to Indraprastha with those two, Vāsudeva had Yudhiṣṭhira perform the great sacrifice, the Rājasūya.
When the sacrifice was concluded there, he gave the foremost worship to Kṛṣṇa with the consent of Bhīṣma.
There, Śiśupāla uttered many words of censure against Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa too cut off his head with Sudarśana.
At the conclusion of three births, he attained conformity of form with Hari.
Then, hearing that Śiśupāla had been slain, Dantavaktra came to Mathurā to fight with Kṛṣṇa.
Hearing that, Kṛṣṇa mounted his chariot and went to Mathurā to fight with him.
A battle took place day and night between Dantavaktra and Vāsudeva at the gate of the city of Mathurā on the bank of the Yamunā. And Kṛṣṇa struck him down with his mace.
With all his limbs shattered, like a mountain split by a thunderbolt, he fell lifeless onto the surface of the earth.
He too attained intimate union with Hari—the supreme, eternal abode of perpetual bliss, accessible to yogis.

In this way Jaya and Vijaya, under the pretext of the curse of Sanaka and the others, descended into worldly existence solely for the sake of the Lord's divine play; and slain across three births by him alone, they attained liberation at the end of the three births.

Having slain him, Kṛṣṇa crossed the Yamunā, went to Nanda's cowherd settlement, greeted his former parents, and consoled them; embraced by them around the neck with tears, he bowed to all the elder cowherds, consoled them, and gratified the inhabitants there with jeweled ornaments and the like.
On the delightful sandbank of the Kālindī, surrounded by sacred trees, / Keśava sported unceasingly with the cowherd women.
Taking the guise of a cowherd through the sheer delight of lovely sport, / Hari, binding the essence of love, dwelt there for two months.

Then all the people dwelling there—Nandagopa and the others, accompanied by their sons and wives, as well as the livestock, birds, wild animals, and others—assumed divine forms through the grace of Vāsudeva, mounted celestial chariots, and attained the supreme realm of Vaikuṇṭha.

Having bestowed his own supreme, sorrowless realm upon all the inhabitants of Nandagopa's settlement, Kṛṣṇa, praised in heaven by the hosts of gods, entered the glorious Dvāravatī.

There, worshiped daily by Vasudeva, Ugrasena, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Akrūra, and others, with sixteen thousand wives

divine queens, he, bearing the universal form, in various chambers made of divine jewels, on very smooth couches adorned with delightful flowers,
reveled.

Now, a Brahmin classmate of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, a childhood friend who was constantly tormented by extreme poverty, tying up a mere handful of parched grains obtained by begging in a ragged cloth, came to the glorious city of Dvārakā to see Vāsudeva.

He stood silent for a moment at the door of Rukmiṇī's inner chambers.

Kṛṣṇa, knowing that a Brahmin had arrived, bowed along with Pradyumna, took his left hand, and seated him on his own seat inside the chamber.
As he trembled with fear, [Kṛṣṇa] washed his feet with water from a golden vessel held in Rukmiṇī's hand and honored him with an offering of honey-mixture.

Having satisfied him with food, drinks, and the like resembling nectar, [Kṛṣṇa] himself took with his own hand the parched grains obtained by begging inside his ragged cloth, and ate them with a laugh.
As the parched grains were eaten by Kṛṣṇa, at that very moment immense prosperity arose for him, consisting of abundant wealth, grain, garments, and ornaments.

Dismissed by Kṛṣṇa, he entered his own town, thinking: 'Neither cloth nor wealth was given to me by Kṛṣṇa.'

Then, seeing his house filled with abundant wealth and grain, saying, “This was obtained through his grace,” with a delighted inner soul,

garments, ornaments, and the like, he enjoyed all desires with his wife; having performed many sacrifices for the satisfaction of Hari, through his grace
he attained the supreme, eternal bliss of heaven.

Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son Duryodhana, having seized the kingdom from the sons of Pāṇḍu under the pretext of a fraudulent dice game, banished them from his realm.

They—Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Arjuna, Nakula, and Sahadeva—together with their good wife Draupadī, went to the great wilderness and there for twelve

dwelt; and having lived incognito for the space of a year in the dwelling of Virāṭa, ruler of the Matsya country,
they came with Vāsudeva as their ally to fight the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

Between those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and sons of Pāṇḍu, along with kings of various lands, a great battle took place on the deeply sacred Kurukṣetra, terrifying even to the gods.

Then the illustrious Kṛṣṇa, acting as Arjuna's charioteer, entered his own power into Arjuna, and through him [slew]

accompanied by the force of eleven army corps, on Kurukṣetra, and having established the Pāṇḍavas in the kingdom,
he completely removed the entire burden of the earth and entered his own city.
Now, after some time, one day a Vedic Brahmin took his dead five-year-old boy, placed him at the king's gate, and weeping profusely, spoke many words of reproach to Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa, hearing that reproach, remained silent.
He said: 'Five of my sons were killed before, and this is the sixth. If Kṛṣṇa does not bring him back to life, then I will die at the king's gate.'
At that time Arjuna, who had come to see Kṛṣṇa, saw him weeping in such a manner out of grief for his son.
Seeing the five-year-old boy who had fallen under the sway of death, Arjuna too was overcome with compassion, granted fearlessness to the Brahmin, and promised: 'I will revive your son.'

Consoled by him, the Brahmin rejoiced.

Then, having consecrated this Brahmin child with many life-restoring weapons and seeing that he had not recovered life, [Arjuna], realizing his vow had been in vain and overcome with great sorrow,
he wished to abandon his life right then.

Kṛṣṇa, knowing all that, came out from the inner apartments and said to that Vedic Brahmin: 'I will give back all your sons.' Having spoken thus and consoled him, he mounted Garuḍa and, together with Arjuna, went to the realm of Viṣṇu.
There, seeing Nārāyaṇa seated together with the Goddess in a divine jeweled pavilion, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna bowed.
Embracing them both with his arms, he said: 'For what purpose have you two come?'
And Kṛṣṇa said: 'O Blessed Lord, give me the sons of the Vedic Brahmin.'
And Nārāyaṇa handed over the Brahmin's sons, abiding at that very age, to Kṛṣṇa.
The illustrious Kṛṣṇa placed them on Garuḍa's shoulders, filled with joy along with Arjuna, mounted himself, and praised in heaven by the hosts of gods, entered Dvāravatī.
He gave the six sons, all at the age of five years, to that Brahmin; and he, filled with supreme joy, gave a blessing: 'May you prosper, O Kṛṣṇa!'
Arjuna, having achieved the fulfillment of his vow, bowed to Kṛṣṇa and went to his own city protected by Yudhiṣṭhira.
Of Kṛṣṇa, ten thousand and a hundred thousand sons were born to his sixteen thousand wives. It is not possible to state the count of their sons and grandsons.
On this point there is also a verse: / 'Eight hundred, thousands, and ten thousand were the sons; / the first of them all was Pradyumna, the son of Rukmiṇī.'
With those innumerable Yādavas, this earth became crowded.
Once again, fearing the burden of the earth, Kṛṣṇa wished to destroy them under the pretext of a curse of the sages.

Once all the youths came to sport at the Narmadā.

Seeing the great sage Kaṇva performing austerities there, they dressed Jāmbavatī's son in woman's attire, tied an iron club to his belly, and [approached] the sage.
all bowed down, placed the youth Sāmba, who was in the form of a wife, before him, and said: "Tell us, will there be a girl or a boy in her womb?"
He, knowing that in his mind and not tolerating [it], said to them all: "May you all be killed by this iron club!"
All, with agitated minds, went to Kṛṣṇa and reported the deed spoken by the great ṛṣi.
Kṛṣṇa too reduced that iron club to powder and threw it into the lake.
From the seeds produced from that iron powder arose great reeds resembling thunderbolts.
There, a fish swallowed the remnant of that club, merely the size of the little finger; a hunter caught that fish, took the piece of the club lying in its belly, and made it the tip of an arrow.

Once all the Yādavas, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Pradyumna, and the rest, having drunk the liquor sent by Indra, became intoxicated. / Taking reeds against one another and speaking many words of abuse, they fought and went to destruction.
Kṛṣṇa, exhausted from the battle, lay down in the shade of a wish-fulfilling tree; that hunter, taking his bow and arrow, went hunting.

In this way, all of them gave up their lives completely; they all reached their respective gods.

Having thus destroyed everything by means of the club, the one God himself slept in the shade of a great tree thick with many bushes.
Contemplating himself whose nature had merged into Vāsudeva, placing one foot upon his knee, he sat down wishing to discard his human form.
In the meantime, the hunter, living by hunting, by the power of Time, seeing Hari's lotus foot—most crimson and marked with the discus, thunderbolt, flag, goad, and other signs—pierced it.
Immediately after, recognizing Śrī Kṛṣṇa, afflicted with great fear and trembling, he folded his hands and bowed down to him, saying: "May my entire great offense be forgiven!"
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, seeing him in such a state, raised him with both hands full of nectar and, consoling him who was afflicted with great fear, spoke, saying: "No offense has been committed by you."

Then he granted him the realm of Viṣṇu, reachable by yogins, free from return, eternal, and full of all the Upaniṣads.

At that very moment, abandoning his human form, he—composed of the five Upaniṣads, accompanied by all his sons and wives—entered the luminous,
world, mounting a divine celestial vehicle resembling the brilliance of a thousand suns, crowded with celestial nymphs, golden, [known as] the sole Vāsudeva.
At that time, Dāruka mounted his chariot and approached Viṣṇu.
Kṛṣṇa sent him, saying: "Bring Arjuna first, who is my own form."
Mounting the chariot swift as thought, he went to Arjuna.
In the meantime, the divine Arjuna mounted it, went around [it], bowed, and, folding his hands, said: "What shall I do?"
Kṛṣṇa said to him: "O Pārtha, I shall go to my own realm. But you, going to Dvāravatī, bring the eight wives residing there, Rukmiṇī and the others, and send them to my body."
He came to the city together with Dāruka.
In the meantime, the gods situated in vehicles in the sky, seeing Kṛṣṇa wishing to go to the heavenly world, praised him along with the ṛṣis and showered rains of flowers.

Kṛṣṇa too, abandoning his human body, assumed his healthy body of the nature of Vāsudeva—the cause of the maintenance and destruction of the entire universe, the inner ruler of every knower of the field, the object of meditation for yogins—and, mounting the son of Vinatā, departed while being praised by the great ṛṣis.
Arjuna related all of that to Vasudeva and Ugrasena, and to the chief queens, Rukmiṇī and the others.

Hearing that, all the citizens and women left Dvāravatī, came out from the inner apartments, and all those beloveds of Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Vasudeva and Ugrasena, went quickly to Hari.

And Revatī, embracing the body of Balabhadra, entered the fire, and having attained a body there, mounted a divine celestial vehicle
and reached the husband's place, the divine realm of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Likewise Rukmin's daughter with Pradyumna, and Uṣā with Aniruddha, and all the Yādava women worshiped their respective husbands' bodies and entered the fire.
Arjuna performed the funeral rites for all of them.
At that time Dāruka too arrived, mounting a divine chariot named Sugrīva, yoked with divine horses and endowed with all jewels.
The pārijāta tree and the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods returned to the world of Indra, the lord of the gods.
At that time the city of Dvāravatī sank into the great ocean.

Then, as all the sixteen thousand wives were going to Indraprastha with Arjuna, bandits seized them.

Formerly, the wives of gods and Gandharvas laughed seeing the great sage Aṣṭāvakra; then cursed by him: "You shall become courtesans!"

he was propitiated and honored, and through his favor, even after obtaining as their husband Vāsudeva who is bowed to by all the worlds, they fell into the hands of bandits because of that very [curse].

Arjuna, defeated by the bandits and overcome with grief, thinking: "The strength of my arms and my valor, along with all my sovereignty, have departed with Kṛṣṇa alone; today my fortune is destroyed," returned to his own city, his splendor completely lost, like the sun at twilight.

Having thus descended into the Yadu lineage for the welfare of all the gods and for the destruction of the entire burden of the earth, [and having] destroyed all the demons,

having destroyed even the great burden of the earth, he liberated the inhabitants of Nanda's cowherd settlement, Dvārakā, and Mathurā—

and immobile beings—from the bonds of time and worldly existence, and having established [them] in the supreme, eternal sovereignty, accessible to yogins, golden, delightful, and sattvic,
Vāsudeva dwelt [there], ever served by his divine chief queens and others.
Here are the verses: / All others may be incarnations, but the life of Kṛṣṇa is great; / the Lord of Ramā manifested to destroy the burden of the earth.
This is the deed of Kṛṣṇa, for the destruction of the wicked; / Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of compassion, rejoices eternally in Vaikuṇṭha.
This most wonderful, auspicious story of Kṛṣṇa, O goddess, / has been told by me in summary, bestowing all fruits upon you.
Whoever recites the deeds of Vāsudeva in the presence of Hari, / or remembers or hears them with devotion, goes to the supreme abode.
Whether endowed with great sins or endowed with minor sins, / by hearing the deeds of the child Kṛṣṇa, one is freed from sins.
Remembering Hari seated in Dvāravatī together with Rukmiṇī, / one undoubtedly attains great sovereignty through this.
In battle, in distress, in an impassable fort, when surrounded by enemies, / by meditating on the leader of all the gods, one will become victorious.
Whoever remembers him sporting with the cowherd maidens in the auspicious cowherd village / attains all desires and indeed finds good fortune.
He who is afflicted by severe troubles, diseases, and the like, [should remember] the eternal [Lord], / who defeated the extremely dreadful kṛtyā-demon who resided in the city of Kāśī.
What is the use of saying much here? At all times, and in the water, O auspicious one, / the wise person should recite the mantra: 'Reverence to Kṛṣṇa.'
'To Kṛṣṇa, to Vāsudeva, to Hari, the Supreme Self, / to Govinda, for the destruction of afflictions, bowing down, reverence, reverence!'
Chanting this mantra every day with devotion, O goddess, / a person, freed from all sins, will attain the world of Viṣṇu.
That Janārdana is indeed the lord of all the gods; / for the protection of the worlds, he truly assumes different states.
Desiring to destroy Tripura, Hari was worshipped by me; / assuming the form of the Buddha, the glorious Lord deluded his enemies.
Deluded by that doctrine, deprived of all dharma, / the enemies of the gods were slain by me with the Nārāyaṇa weapon.
Incarnating at the end of the Kali [age] in the dwelling of a brāhmaṇa, / Janārdana will likewise destroy all the terrible barbarians.
All the states of the Lord of the universe through various manifestations have been declared by me. / What else do you wish to hear? That I shall tell, O fair-faced one.

6.253.m: Śrī Pārvatī said: / O Blessed One, everything regarding the state of Hari's majestic power has been declared. / In this, the narrative of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa was exceedingly wondrous.
Ah! Even through hundreds of different kalpas, / as I hear the life of Rāma and of the great-souled Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of the gods,

my mind finds no satiation at all, O Lord of beings, in the nectar of Hari's tales. / Now I wish to hear the supreme glorification of Viṣṇu, / and likewise, O god, I wish to hear the rules for his worship.
Śrī Rudra said: / Listen, O goddess, I shall explain [the worship] of Hari, the great-souled one; / it is celebrated as two kinds: installed and self-manifest.
Having fashioned an image of Hari out of stone, clay, wood, metal, and the like, / that installation performed with rituals declared by the Vedas, Smṛtis, and Āgamas,
is said to be 'installed'; but hear from me what is 'self-manifest': / where Viṣṇu is directly present on earth for men on his own,
in stone or wood, the Lord being its very self—that is known as 'self-manifest'. / One should worship Madhusūdana whether self-manifest or installed.
For the purpose of being worshipped by the deities and the great seers, the eternal Keśava, / the Lord of the universe, himself becomes directly present.
Whatever image was fit to be enjoyed by whom, that very one appeared on earth; / that very one he should always worship, and in that very one he should constantly delight.
The Lord of the gods reclining at Śrīraṅga, the best of the gods, is to be worshipped according to rule; / he alone appeared on earth through the ascetic practice of the Ikṣvāku lords.
In Kāśī as well, Mādhava, who removes impurity, is to be worshipped by me. / Wherever in a delightful house the eternal [Lord] is self-manifest,
there I go and dwell, taking delight. / Not through the eightfold yoga is the Lord of sacrifice found by men as he is in an image;
coming within the range of their eyes, he grants the desired boon. / Easy accessibility in all circumstances is attained by people through the image;
his presence is always available even to the ignorant on the surface of the earth. / In Jambūdvīpa, in the greatly meritorious, auspicious Bhārata realm,
Viṣṇu is present in the image, never in other [realms]. / Therefore, in the Bhārata realm, by sages and even by gods,
he is constantly served, O goddess, with asceticism, sacrifice, rituals, and the like. / In this great Bhārata realm, Hari is perpetually present:
at Indradyumna, likewise at Kūrma, on Siṃhādri, at Karavīra, / in Kāśī, at Prayāga the charming, and on Śālagrāma mountain,
at Dvāravatī, and in Naimiṣa, likewise at Badarikāśrama, / at Kṛtaśauca he removes sin, and at Pauṇḍarīka, and in Daṇḍaka,
in Mathurā, and on Veṅkaṭādri, on Śvetādri, on Garuḍādri, / in Kāñcī, at Anantaśayana, at Śrīraṅga, on Vāsavādri,
on Nārāyaṇādri the pleasant, at Vārāha, at Vāmanāśrama; / such are the primary self-manifest places granting the fruit of all desires.
Where Janārdana himself indeed manifests his presence, / only in that [case] do the auspicious sages call it 'self-manifest'.
A best of great devotees, having installed Keśava according to rule, / should establish his presence by means of mantra; that installation is distinguished.
In that [image] one should worship the god in villages and in houses. / But on the Śālagrāma stone household worship is approved by the virtuous:
worship, chanting of mantras, the sacrificial rite and yoga of the great-souled one, / chanting his names, service, marking oneself with his emblems,
and the veneration of his devotees—this is ninefold, O auspicious one. / The performance of those particular rituals is perpetually prescribed for the brāhmaṇa.
The best great devotee, a brāhmaṇa, is truly the teacher of men; / by all the worlds he is to be worshipped just as Hari is.
Endowed with the five sacraments beginning with branding, performing the rites of ninefold worship, / knowing the five realities, a brāhmaṇa is known as a great devotee.
Worship through the performance of those particular rites is prescribed for the kṣatriya; / marking with his emblems, service, and worship of his devotees,
chanting the syllables of the mantra, singing Hari's names, / and prostration are declared for the vaiśya by the rule of sixfold worship.
Chanting the names, service, worship, and prostration, / and veneration of his devotees—[this] is the fivefold worship for one born as a śūdra.
Common to all men, O beloved, is mental worship, / and worship of the Lord of the universe should be performed according to one's qualification,
by those devoted to no other deity, seeking no other fruit, / knowing the Veda, knowing the reality of Brahman, free from passion, seekers of liberation,
endowed with devotion to the guru, deeply serene, truly virtuous, / by brāhmaṇas and by others as well, Hari is always to be worshipped.
Worship of Hari is to be performed by men according to what is appropriate for their caste, / and auspicious Vaiṣṇavas must act in accordance with caste and stage of life.
One should properly and constantly practice here what is declared by Śruti and Smṛti; / a wise man should not transgress the duties stated in Śruti and Smṛti.
A Vaiṣṇava who does not follow the conduct stated in Śruti and Smṛti / becomes a heretic and will dwell in the Raurava hell.
Therefore, one should perform the worship of the Lord of the universe in accordance with one's caste; / therefore, a person should always follow the conduct stated in the Smṛti.
Indeed, mental worship is common to all men, O auspicious one; / only having observed one's own qualification should one perform action unweariedly.
Tranquility, self-restraint, asceticism, purity, truth, abstention from meat, / non-stealing, and non-violence are the means of dharma for all.
Therefore, one should worship Madhusūdana in accordance with one's caste. / Rising at the end of the night, having sipped water according to rule,
bowing to one's gurus, one should remember Acyuta in one's heart; / restrained in speech and pure, one should praise [him] with devotion through the thousand names.
Going outside the village, [reciting] the root mantra according to the rule, / having performed cleansing according to proper method and sipped water, restrained and pure,
he should indeed perform his bath preceded by cleaning the teeth according to rule, / taking soil from the root of a tulasī plant together with its leaves.
Consecrating it with the root mantra and with the Gāyatrī, O fair-faced one, / his body smeared by that very mantra, he should bathe after performing Aghamarṣaṇa.
Invoking the Gaṅgā, which arose from Hari's foot, into that very clear [water], / having submerged himself, he should quickly mutter the supreme Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
Having sipped water, he should perform sprinkling according to the order spoken in the Puruṣasūkta; / then, having plunged in quickly, the wise man should mutter the root mantra,
either twenty-eight times, or one hundred and eight times. / Having consecrated the water with the mantra, the Vaiṣṇava should then pray to it.
Having sipped water, he should offer libations to the gods, the sages, and likewise the ancestors; / having wrung out his garment and sipped water, clothed in a washed garment,
taking pure, pleasant clay, the best of the twice-born, / having consecrated it with the mantra, the Vaiṣṇava, on the forehead and other limbs,
should apply the vertical sectarian marks according to the prescribed number, unwearied. / Having properly attended upon the twilight devotion, the wise man should mutter the Sāvitrī.
Self-controlled, going home, washing his feet, with restrained speech, / having sipped water, he should enter the worship pavilion with a focused mind.
On a pleasant, very bright seat adorned with a heap of flowers, / having placed upon it that lord, the divine Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa,

he should worship him properly according to the rule with perfume, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and the like, / whether in an installed image, a self-manifest one, or in household worship, according to the injunction.
The twice-born, with attentive mind, should perform the worship of Viṣṇu / spoken of in the Śrauta, Smārta, and Āgama texts, with devotion and according to his capacity.
As instructed by his guru, so should the Vaiṣṇava act: / the Śrauta is declared to be Vaikhānasa, the Smārta is said to be Vāsiṣṭha,
and the Pañcarātra rite is declared to be the divine Āgama. / There must be no omission of rites; worship of Viṣṇu is supreme.
With invocation, seat, water for respectful offering, and so forth, with perfume, flowers, unbroken grains, and the like, / with incenses, lamps, food offerings, betel, and prostrations,
the Vaiṣṇava, filled with joy, should perform the worship of Viṣṇu to the best of his ability, / stanza by stanza with the Puruṣasūkta and with the root mantra.
He should perform [the worship] with both mantras through the sixteen services; / further, at each service, he should then offer a handful of flowers.
The Vaiṣṇava should invoke the Lord of the Universe with the gesture, / and he should present the seat with the flower gesture.
Lamp, water for respectful offering, sipping water, and bathing, with clear waters placed in vessels, / combined with auspicious substances and mixed with tulasī leaves,
he should offer at each service with the pair of root mantras; / then he should perform the smearing with fragrant oil.
He should also perform the rubbing and the rest with musk and sandalwood; / having bathed [the deity] with auspicious waters scented with sweet perfumes and accompanied by mantras,
having adorned him according to rule with garments and celestial ornaments, / he should then offer honey-mixture and offer fragrant perfume.
He should properly offer sweet-smelling, fine flowers with devotion, / incense composed of ten or eight ingredients, and a very charming lamp.
He should offer various foods mixed with rice pudding and sweet cakes; / and he should offer camphor along with betel with devotion.
Having performed the wave-offering with lamps, he should worship with a garland of flowers; / having circumambulated, prostrated, and praised him with unexcelled hymns,
having laid him down upon the lap of Garuḍa, he should offer the auspicious respectful offering; / having praised him with sacred names, he should afterwards perform the fire offering.
With the remnant of Hari's food offering, he should make oblations into the circle of fire, / stanza by stanza with the Puruṣasūkta and the Śrīsūkta entitled the auspicious.
It should be offered mixed with clarified butter, as sacrificial food into the Vedic fire; / he should offer it with devotion, using the declared jewel among mantras,
one hundred and eight times, or indeed twenty-eight times, / meditating upon Mahāviṣṇu, who is the embodiment of sacrifice, as he offers the sacrificial food:
resembling pure gold, holding the conch, discus, and mace, / the Lord accompanied by all the Vedas and Upaniṣads together with their auxiliary and secondary limbs,
seated together with the goddess Śrī—having thus meditated, he should perform the fire offering; / afterwards, he should offer sacrificial food, oblation by oblation, with the names,
addressing the eternal devotees, the best of the great devotees of the Lord: / first, in order, the powers such as Bhū, Līlā, and Vimalā;
after that, Ananta, the king of birds [Garuḍa], and the other deities; / then Vāsudeva and the rest, and likewise the deities of power and the like;
the forms beginning with Keśava, and likewise Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others; / the Fish, the Tortoise, and the others, and likewise the weapons beginning with the discus;
Kumuda and the other celestials, and likewise deities beginning with the Moon; / the world guardians beginning with Indra, and likewise the deities beginning with Dharma.
Oblations should be made in order to them, and they should be especially worshipped; / this is indeed the Vaikuṇṭha fire offering, which the best of the great devotees of the Lord
should perform daily in the rite of daily worship, with concentrated mind; / in domestic worship, at the door of the house, according to the rule of the five sacrifices,
having given the food offering according to the rule, he should afterwards perform sipping of water; / having sat upon an auspicious seat overlaid with black antelope skin and kuśa grass,
he should engage in mantra-yoga for the enjoyment of his own happiness; / seated properly in the lotus posture, he should perform the purification of the elements.
With senses conquered, he should perform three breath-controls with the mantra; / having then turned upward the supreme lotus of the heart,
he should cause its expansion by means of the sun of wisdom in his heart; / in its pericarp, the discs of fire, sun, and moon in succession—
the best of Vaiṣṇavas should meditate upon this triad consisting of the three Vedas; / above them, he should meditate upon a pedestal made of various gems.

Upon it, at the end of the root of the heart lotus, [he should visualize] an eight-petaled lotus representing the eight powers, / possessing a radiance like the rising sun, composed of the syllables of the mantra.
Upon it, seated with the goddess, resembling ten million cool-rayed moons, / four-armed, with handsome limbs, holding the conch, discus, and mace,
with large eyes like lotus petals, marked with all auspicious marks, / his chest adorned with the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha, the Lord clad in yellow garments,
endowed with varied ornaments, adorned with divine embellishments, / his limbs smeared with divine sandalwood, adorned with celestial flowers,
decorated with a garland of forest flowers and tender tulasī leaves, / equal in splendor to ten million rising suns, along with the goddess Śrī,
whose auspicious body is embraced by her who possesses all auspicious marks; / having thus meditated, he should mutter the mantra with a concentrated mind, being pure,
a thousand times, or a hundred times, or according to his capacity; / having performed worship with the mind alone, he should cease there with devotion.
He should worship His devotees who have arrived at that time with devotion; / having gratified them with food, drink, and the like, he should send them off, accompanying them [a short distance].
Having worshipped the ancestors and gods, he should make libations according to rule; / having honored guests and servants, the husband and wife should eat.
One should always avoid the worship of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and spirits; / the twice-born who performs it out of delusion certainly becomes an outcaste.
The worship of yakṣas and piśācas, and likewise of [such] denizens of heaven / who consume liquor and meat, is traditionally declared equal to drinking liquor.
The worship of brahmarākṣasas, vetālas, yakṣas, and bhūtas by men / is a means to attain the terrifyingly dreadful hell of Kumbhīpāka.
The merit accumulated over ten million births—sacrifices, gifts, rituals, and the like— / instantly dissolves completely from worshipping yakṣas, bhūtas, and the like.
Whether a woman or a man, from worshipping yakṣas, bhūtas, and others, / for hundreds of millions of kalpas and thousands of millions of kalpas,
becomes a worm in feces and sinks together with their ancestors. / Of yakṣas, piśācas, and tamasic deities,
whoever eats food offered [to them] becomes an eater of pus and blood. / Any Brahmin who eats food dedicated to yakṣas,
the hosts of bhūtas, or other cruel brahmarākṣasas, instantly becomes an outcaste. / Any woman who worships yakṣas, piśācas, serpents, or rākṣasas,
goes head-down to the dreadful hell of Kālasūtra. / Having dwelt there in that terrible place with her ancestors until the end of a kalpa,
licking urine and feces with torment, and eaten by needle-mouthed / worms in every limb until the cosmic dissolution,
she is later born on earth in the hundreds within intervals of ten days. / Therefore, one should abandon the worship of yakṣas and other such deities.
Where one should abandon independent worship even of Vedic [deities], / after worshipping the god Nārāyaṇa, Hari, praiseworthy by the world.
one should then worship the surrounding deities situated in his enclosure all around. / One should cast the bali to them with the remnants of what Hari has eaten.
A Vaiṣṇava should perform the fire offering with the very remnant of that; / he should offer oblation to the gods only as properly dedicated to Hari.
He should also give that to the ancestors; he will obtain everything imperishable. / Tormenting living beings, O wise ones, surely leads to hell.
Whatever of another's property is taken by men when not given, / know that to be theft, O daughter of the mountain, a direct cause of hell.
Garlic, drinking intoxicants, radish, likewise red garlic, / sesame paste, moringa, bilva fruit, and sponge gourd,
gourd, eggplant, citron, and wild cabbages— / eating these and other uneatables seen in the scriptures,
a man attains a varied and dreadful hell. / And the food of non-Vaiṣṇavas and fallen persons,
as well as whatever is unoffered to Viṣṇu, is equal to dog meat. / The food of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and bhūtas, spirituous liquor, wine, and red garlic—
he who eats them goes to hell, eating pus and blood. / By lodging, contact, and living together with these persons, O man,
they too go straight to hell, eating feces, urine, and worms. / Through association with fallen persons and heretics,
knowing the ancient Supreme Person to be the enjoyer of every sacrifice, / one should perform all daily and occasional rites.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, kūṣmāṇḍa retinues, and bhairavas / are never to be worshipped, O goddess, by those desiring heaven.
A twice-born person should avoid worshipping yakṣas, rākṣasas, and bhūtas; / [otherwise] he attains the state of a piśāca for three hundred million kalpas.
Therefore, worshipping rākṣasas and bhūtas is forbidden. / For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas,
one goes to the Raurava hell through worshipping the hosts of yakṣas and bhūtas. / Lacking the conch, discus, and other marks dearest to Hari,
and fallen from all dharmas, one goes to hell. / From approaching illicit women, from violence, and from taking another's property,
and from eating uneatables, one directly attains hell. / He who abandons his wedded wife and goes to another woman—
that is indeed approaching an illicit woman, an immediate cause of hell. / Through association with fallen persons, heretics,
and those engaged in wrong actions, a man surely goes to hell. / One should avoid association with such companions, and even contact with them.
A Vaiṣṇava should avoid an entire family endowed with sin; / an exclusive devotee should abandon a village mixed with great sins;
likewise, a supreme exclusive devotee should even abandon that country. / The means consisting of one's own duty, knowledge, and devotion is considered the Vaiṣṇava way.
The Brahmin who practices work, knowledge, and the rest in accordance with Hari's command, / devoted to Vāsudeva, becomes an exclusive devotee.
A Vaiṣṇava should completely abandon what is forbidden, knowing it to be sin; / an exclusive devotee should abandon even in mind any teaching that causes fault;
likewise, a supreme exclusive devotee should abandon it, knowing it to be entirely rejected. / Required duty is known to be of three kinds: regular, occasional, and optional;
similarly, knowledge in this world is proclaimed by the sages to be / discernment between what should and should not be done, contemplation of the other world,
the means of attaining that, and knowledge of the essential nature of Viṣṇu. / A devotee should be endowed with devotion; it is proclaimed to be of nine kinds:
auspicious marking with his signs such as the Sudarśana and the vertical sectarian mark, / recitation of the mantra of a true guru, ritual worship of Hari according to the rules,
remembrance and chanting of Viṣṇu, service to the Supreme Self, / prostration before him, worship of his devotees,
and taking his grace and holy water—this is considered ninefold devotion. / Since a Vaiṣṇava seeks refuge in the god Hari,
surrender is to be known as proclaimed in three kinds: / it is considered three kinds—tamasic, rajasic, and sattvic.
Accomplishment made threefold is common to all embodied beings. / O goddess, a Vaiṣṇava, abandoning this tetrad as something to be renounced,
should rely upon Brahman itself, which is the Vaiṣṇava means. / Relinquishing action, knowledge, and the rest as the ultimate means,
the best of great devotees should act for the satisfaction of the Lord. / One should worship Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, with devotion at the three junctures of the day.
He should especially worship him according to rule on auspicious occasional observances. / Every day in the month of Kārttika, he should worship him with jasmine flowers,
and with restrained mind and firm vow, offer an unbroken lamp. / Having fed Brahmins, at the end he attains union with Hari.
In Sagittarius at dawn, for an entire month without interruption, / one should worship the Lord of the gods, O goddess, with blue water-lilies and white and red oleanders,
and offer incense, lamps, and food offerings according to one's means. / At the conclusion, one should feed the best of great devotees among Brahmins;
he attains the fruit of a thousand horse sacrifices without doubt. / In the month of Māgha, having bathed especially in a river when the sun rises,
one should worship Mādhava with flowers and blue water-lilies, O fair-faced one, / and offer there with devotion divine milk-rice enriched with ghee.
Having bathed, one should worship Viṣṇu continuously for an entire month, / and offer daily a garden of delicacies with sugar water.
He should worship Vaiṣṇavas with devotion at the end of the month, O lovely-looking one. / In the month of Caitra likewise, continuously with bakula and campaka flowers,
he should worship the Lord of the worlds and offer food cooked with molasses. / At the end of the month, well composed, he should feed Vaiṣṇava Brahmins;
he obtains daily the reward of worship lasting a thousand years. / In the month of Vaiśākha, he should worship the God with lotuses and great blue water-lilies.
Having worshipped according to rule, he should offer with devotion / curd-rice mixed with fruits, and water sweetened with molasses, O goddess, to him.
United with Lakṣmī, the Lord of the World becomes pleased, O Pārvatī. / In the month of Jyeṣṭha, however, with white lotuses, trumpet flowers, and water lilies,
having worshiped Hṛṣīkeśa and offered food accompanied by mango fruits / with devotion indeed, one obtains the merit of giving ten million cows.
Then, having fed the Vaiṣṇavas, he attains all that is infinite. / In the month of Āṣāḍha, [having worshiped] Acyuta, the Lord of the god of gods, the husband of Lakṣmī,
one should worship him daily with Śrī-flowers and offer milk-rice food; / at the end of the month, one should feed the best of the great devotees of Bhagavān, the brāhmaṇas.
He obtains the fruit of sixty thousand years of worship; there is no doubt. / In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship Viṣṇu with punnāga flowers and screw-pine petals.
Having worshiped Acyuta with devotion, he does not take birth again. / Then he should offer with devotion rice cakes mixed with sugar and ghee;
in the same way he should feed brāhmaṇas: he attains all that is infinite. / In the month of Bhādrapada, too, he should worship the Lord with jasmine and red amaranth flowers;
he should offer there with devotion milk-rice mixed with molasses: / every day he obtains the fruit of giving ten million cows.
In the month of Āśvina, one should worship Madhusūdana with blue lotuses; / with devotion one should offer him milk mixed with cakes.
For thousands of crores of kalpas and hundreds of crores of kalpas, / he reaches the realm of Viṣṇu, rejoiced and surrounded by his kin.
Likewise in the month of Kārttika, O goddess, with tender leaves of tulasī, / having worshiped Acyuta with devotion, he attains absorption into him.
Food endowed with milk, ghee, and sugar, and likewise pāyasa, / and cake, in proper order indeed, he should properly offer with devotion.
On the new moon, on Saturday, and on a Vaiṣṇava asterism, / at the sun's transit, on vyatīpāta, and at an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
one should worship Viṣṇu especially, according to one's ability, O fair-faced woman; / on the day of the spiritual teacher's departure, and on the birth constellations of Hari,
the best of the twice-born should also perform a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice according to his ability. / There he should offer a handful of flowers measured by the Veda before each image.
And he should perform the breaking of the fast with sacrificial cooked grain or with milk-rice; / he should feed the Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇas and give a sacrificial fee according to his capacity.
Having delivered ten million of his lineage, he attains the state of Viṣṇu. / If one is unable to worship the supreme devotee of Bhagavān with all the Vedas,
one should offer a thousand handfuls of flowers and perform homa daily / for seven nights continuously with Vaiṣṇava hymns;
or, for the pleasure of Bhagavān, the wise man may sacrifice at each verse. / Alternatively, for seven nights continuously, with the jewel of mantras,
he should offer one thousand and eight oblations with ghee and sacrifice. / The wise man should especially worship the best of the great devotees of Bhagavān,
and at the conclusion he should perform the final ablution according to the extent of his wealth. / And the twice-born should perform the final ablution with Vaiṣṇava hymns.
Having bathed here according to the rule according to his ability, the best of the twice-born, / having washed their feet with devotion in another auspicious, delightful vessel,
should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and the like, with garments, ornaments, and so forth; / he should thoroughly worship them according to his capacity with betel or with fruits.
Having fed them with food, drink, and the like, and having bowed again and again, / following them to the boundary and having saluted, they are dismissed.
Having bowed again with devotion, then turning back slowly from there, / entering his house, with a restrained mind, he should worship the Lord of gods.
In this way he should worship Viṣṇu all his life without laxity; / and, O auspicious one, he should always especially worship those who belong to him.
Of all forms of adoration, the adoration of Viṣṇu is supreme; / higher even than that, O goddess, is the worship of those who belong to him.
Though having worshiped Govinda, if one does not worship those who belong to him, / he is not to be known as a devotee of Bhagavān; he is remembered merely as a hypocrite.
Therefore a man should always worship the Vaiṣṇavas with effort; / from the worship of the great devotees of Bhagavān, he crosses over the entire flood of sorrow.
Thus has been spoken by me, O goddess, the supreme adoration of Viṣṇu, / both regular and occasional, and the worship of those who belong to him;

his human true nature, the fruit and the means, / and his bodily dwelling, and the fourfold division beginning with action— / [all this] has been told to you by me, O goddess. What else do you wish to hear?

6.254.m: Vasiṣṭha said: / Having been addressed thus by her husband, the spear-holder, the goddess / then bowed down to the great soul and, with folded hands, said:
Pārvatī said: / Well spoken indeed by you, O lord, is the supreme Vaiṣṇava duty, / the secret of secrets, the true nature of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self.
I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, O you who are bowed to by all the gods! / By your grace I shall worship the eternal Lord of the gods.
Vasiṣṭha said: / Then, having heard that speech of hers, Bhava, the destroyer of Tripura, / embraced the goddess and spoke with a joyful inner self:
Rudra said: / Well done, well done, O great goddess! Well done, well done, O fair-faced woman! / Worship Hṛṣīkeśa, the husband of Lakṣmī, Acyuta.
I have accomplished my purpose, O auspicious one, through you, a Vaiṣṇava wife! / With permission from your spiritual teacher, the wise Vāmadeva, O fair-limbed woman,

worship the Lord, the ancient Supreme Person. / Only by worshiping Keśava in accordance with the path of the spiritual teacher's instruction / does one obtain all that is desired, not otherwise, O daughter of the mountain!
Vasiṣṭha said: / Addressed thus at that time, O king, the goddess went quickly to the presence of Vāmadeva, / delighted and eager to worship Viṣṇu.
Approaching that spiritual teacher, O king, having worshiped and bowed down, / humble and with folded hands, the goddess spoke to that best of sages:
Pārvatī said: / O venerable one, by your grace I shall perform the complete adoration of Hari, / O best of the twice-born; you ought to grant permission.
Vasiṣṭha said: / Addressed thus by that goddess, Vāmadeva, the great sage, / the spiritual teacher, gave her that best, supreme mantra according to the rule.
And the best of sages spoke the thousand names of Viṣṇu. / Having taught also the rule of worship, the spiritual teacher / spoke with supreme affection to Pārvatī, who was firm in her vows:
Vāmadeva said: / Having worshiped Hṛṣīkeśa every day in the morning, O fair-faced woman, / perform the recitation of the thousand names immediately after that.
Vasiṣṭha said: / Addressed in this way by that spiritual teacher with a joyful inner self, / having worshiped and bowed to him, she returned again to her own abode.
Pārvatī was thus instructed by that spiritual teacher, Vāmadeva. / Then, after a few days, on the twelfth lunar day, the bull-bannered Lord,
Śaṅkara, having worshiped Viṣṇu on the delightful peak of Kailāsa, / sat down then to eat. Śaṅkara said to Pārvatī:
Śaṅkara said: / O Pārvatī, come to eat along with me, O woman praised by the world! / Vasiṣṭha said: To him the goddess Pārvatī said: 'Having chanted the thousand names,
only then shall I eat, O god; let it be eaten by you, O lord.' / Then, laughing gently, the Supreme Lord said to that Pārvatī:

Śaṃkara said:
You are blessed, you have accomplished your aim, you are a devotee of Viṣṇu, O Pārvatī. / Devotion to Viṣṇu is rare without good fortune, O sovereign lady.
Saying 'Rāma, Rāma, Rāma,' I delight in Rāma, O lovely one; / the name of Rāma is equal to the thousand names, O fair-faced lady.
When I hear names beginning with the syllable 'ra', O Pārvatī, / my mind attains delight out of the anticipation of the name of Rāma.
Having uttered 'Rāma', O great goddess, eat now along with me. / Vasiṣṭha said: Then, having uttered the name 'Rāma', Pārvatī ate together [with him].
Having said 'Rāma', the great goddess, seated together with Śambhu, / asked the god Śaṃkara, her mind full of love and reverent devotion:

Pārvatī said:
You have spoken of the name of Rāma as equal to the thousand names. / If there are other names of that enemy of Rāvaṇa, / let them be told to me, O lord of gods; devotion to him has arisen in me.

The venerable Mahādeva said:
Listen, O Pārvatī, I shall declare the names of Rāmacandra. / Whatever words there are, whether worldly or Vedic, O Pārvatī,
are the names of Rāmacandra, and among them a thousand are superior; / and among those, the one hundred and eight names are exceedingly primary.
Each single name of Viṣṇu is considered superior to all the Vedas; / a thousand such names are equal to the name of Rāma.
Whatever fruit is attained from reciting all the mantras of the Vedas, O dear one, / that fruit, multiplied ten-millionfold, is obtained merely from the name of Rāma.
Hear the principal names of Rāma, O lady of auspicious sight; / sung by the sages, those I shall tell you, O dear one:
—Śrīrāma, Rāmacandra, and Rāmabhadra, the eternal, / the lotus-eyed, the glorious, the king of kings, the eminent of Raghu's line,
the beloved of Jānakī, the victorious, he whose foes are conquered, Janārdana, / beloved of Viśvāmitra, the self-controlled, dedicated to protecting those seeking refuge,
the slayer of Vālin, the eloquent, true in speech, true in valor, / true to his vows, the fruit of vows, always the refuge of Hanumat,
son of Kauśalyā, destroyer of Khara, skilled in killing Virādha, / protector of Vibhīṣaṇa, remover of the heads of the ten-necked [Rāvaṇa],
piercer of the seven palmyra trees, shatterer of Hara's bow, / crusher of the great pride of the son of Jamadagni, and destroyer of Tāḍakā.

He is the end of the Vedānta, the self of the Vedas, the sole remedy for the bondage of worldly existence, / the foe of Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras, the triple form, possessed of the three qualities, the three Vedas;
Trivikrama, the self of the three worlds, he whose pure deeds are celebrated, / the protector of the three worlds, the archer, the dweller in the Daṇḍaka forest;
the purifier of Ahalyā, devoted to his father, the giver of boons, / having subdued his senses, conquered anger, and subdued greed, the teacher of the world;
he who allied with the hosts of bears and monkeys, having his resort at Citrakūṭa, / granting protection and boons to Jayanta, attended by the son of Sumitrā;
the supreme deity of all gods, the reviver of dead monkeys, / the slayer of the illusory Mārīca, most fortunate, mighty-armed;
praised by all gods, gentle, beneficent to brahmins, best among sages, / a great yogin, immensely generous, giver of a stable kingdom to Sugrīva;
yielding fruits superior to all merits, whose remembrance destroys all sins, / the primal Person, the great Person, and the highest Person;
the dawn of merit, the great essence, the ancient Supreme Person, / smiling-faced, measured in speech, first to speak, Rāghava;
profound with infinite qualities, steadfast, elevated by subdued virtues, / having the conduct of an illusory mortal, worshiped by Mahādeva;
builder of the bridge, conqueror of the ocean lord, full of all sacred places, Hari, / dark-bodied, handsome, heroic, clothed in yellow, bearer of the bow;
lord of all sacrifices, sacrifice itself, free from old age and death, / establisher of the liṅga of Śiva, devoid of all material attributes;
the Supreme Self, the supreme Brahman, whose form is being-consciousness-bliss, / the supreme light, the supreme abode, the supreme sky, higher than the high;
the supreme lord, who reaches the other shore, the other shore itself, whose self is all beings, Śiva. / Thus the one hundred and eight names of glorious Rāmacandra,
more secret than the secret, O goddess, have been proclaimed out of love for you. / Whoever reads or even listens to them with a mind joined with devotion,
is freed from all sins born of hundreds of millions of cosmic ages. / Waters turn into dry land; enemies become friends;
kings become servants; fires become gentle; / beings show benevolence; and fickle riches attain stability;
planets grant favor, and afflictions subside / for a man who recites it with a devotional disposition, O daughter of the mountain.
If one recites it with supreme devotion, the three worlds become subject to him. / Whatever desire he forms, he obtains each and every one through this recitation.
For thousands of millions of cosmic ages, and hundreds of millions of cosmic ages, / he rejoices eternally in Vaikuṇṭha with ten preceding and ten following generations.
Those who praise Rāma—dark as a blade of dūrvā grass, lotus-eyed, wearing yellow garments— / with divine names, do not remain mundane men.
“To Rāma, to Rāmabhadra, to Rāmacandra, the Creator, / to the lord of the Raghus, to the master, the husband of Sītā, reverence.”
O great goddess, continually reciting this mantra day and night, / completely freed from all sins, one will attain unity with Viṣṇu.
“Thus, O fair-browed one, the glorification of Rāmacandra, equal to the Veda / and bearing an auspicious name, has indeed been narrated by me out of affection for you.”
Vasiṣṭha said: / Having heard that glorification of the Supreme Self spoken by Śaṅkara, / she experienced unequaled joy, bathed in tears of bliss.

Having bowed down, she addressed her husband, the lord of gods whose banner is a bull: / Pārvatī said: / “Ah, how incomparable is the glorification of Rāma, the Supreme Self! / My ears would not find full satisfaction even in hundreds of tens of thousands of cosmic ages.
Fortunate am I; I have accomplished my purpose. All has been told by you, O sinless one. / By your grace, may I have devotion to Hari birth after birth.”

Vasiṣṭha said: / Having thus spoken to her husband, Gaurī, foremost of devotees of Bhagavān, [reciting:] / “To Rāma, to Rāmabhadra, to Rāmacandra, the Creator, / to the lord of the Raghus, to the master, the husband of Sītā, reverence,”
chanting only this mantra under all circumstances, / Pārvatī dwelt indeed in comfort on Kailāsa with her husband.
All this, the most secret of secrets, has been narrated to you, O king. / The scriptures spoken by Rudra are indeed of the quality of darkness, O ruler of the earth.
In order to bewilder the worlds, he whose banner is a bull spoke them. / But in secret, the powerful Hara declared this single truth to the goddess.
The true meaning, secret, and essence of the mantra, O protector of the earth, / Mahādeva, devoted [to Rāma], related out of love for the goddess.
This wondrous dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, O king, / whoever reads or even listens to it with a mind joined with devotion,
he becomes worshipful to all, all-knowing, a great devotee of Bhagavān; / released from all duties, he reaches the supreme state.
Fortunate indeed are you in the world, O lord of kings, greatly powerful! / In your lineage the glorious Hari, the ancient Supreme Person,

will be born as the son of Daśaratha, verily for the welfare of all the worlds. / Therefore the Ikṣvākus are to be honored even by the gods, O king,

among whom the venerable lotus-eyed Rāma was born.

6.255.m: Dilīpa said: / You have declared to me in full, O brahmin, all dharma, / general and specific, and the true natures of the Supreme and the individual soul.
Heaven and liberation have been explained, and the means to attain them both. / I am blessed, O foremost of the twice-born, by your grace, eternal Guru.
I ask you another thing, O best among the twice-born, out of curiosity; / explain it truthfully, out of affection and honor [for me].
Why did Rudra, the slayer of Tripura, foremost of great devotees of Bhagavān, / along with his wife, take on a reviled form?
And how could the high-souled one have the nature of the womb and the phallus— / he who has five faces, four arms, a trident in hand, and three eyes?
How did he attain that reviled form, O bull among the twice-born? / Explain all this to me, O son of Mitra and Varuṇa.
Vasiṣṭha said: / Listen, O king, I will tell you that which you ask me out of respect; / in the purified heart of men, an understanding regarding the highest good arises.
Formerly, the Svāyambhuva Manu, along with sages on Mandara, the best of mountains, / went to undertake an unsurpassed, extended sacrificial session.
All the sages assembled there were of praised vows, / knowers of various scriptures, preeminent, radiant like the morning sun and fire,
twice-born knowers of all the Vedas, dedicated to all dharma. / While that great sacrificial session was proceeding, the sages whose sins were destroyed,
wishing to investigate the truth about the deity, spoke among themselves, rich in austerities: / “For the twice-born knowers of the Vedas, who is the supreme deity to be worshiped?
Among Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna, who, when praised, grants liberation to men? / Whose foot-water is to be attended upon, and whose food-remnants are purifying?
Who is the imperishable, the supreme abode, the eternal Supreme Self? / By whose grace and sacred water will satisfaction arise for the ancestors?”
Among them as they were seated, a great debate arose. / Some great sages here declared: “Rudra alone!”
Other best of sages said: “Brahmā alone is to be worshiped!” / Other excellent ones declared: “The Sun alone is to be worshiped by souls!”
[Others said:] “He who is all-pervading, glorious, the lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person, / imperishable, lotus-eyed, Vāsudeva, higher than the high!”
"Viṣṇu, without beginning or end, is the Supreme Lord himself, / the foremost of deities to be worshiped"—thus other twice-born ones said.
As they were disputing there, the self-born Manu said: / "He who consists of pure sattva, the lord possessing auspicious qualities,
lotus-eyed, glorious, consort of Śrī, the supreme person, / is the one lord worshiped by brahmins knowledgeable in the Vedas.
Others mixed with rajas and tamas are not to be worshiped by brahmins." / Hearing his words, all the great sages / addressed Bhṛgu, the brahmin treasury of asceticism, with folded hands:

The sages said:
You are capable of resolving our doubt, O one of noble vows; / go, O one of noble vows, into the presence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
Having approached their presence, and having observed their forms, / [see] in whom among them the quality of pure sattva is found, O sage.
He alone is to be worshiped by brahmins, and no other at any time; / he will be composed of pure sattva, directly friendly to brahmins.
He shall possess holy waters and grace in the world for brahmins, / and his leftover offering shall be exceedingly purifying for the deities and ancestors.
Therefore go, O best of sages, to the abode of the gods; / quickly accomplish the welfare of all the worlds, O best of sages, O lord.
Thus addressed, the best of sages then went swiftly to Kailāsa, / where sits the bull-bannered [god] with Vāmadeva.
Approaching the door of the dwelling of the great-souled Śaṃkara, / and seeing the exceedingly fierce Nandin with spear in hand, the twice-born said:
"I, the brahmin Bhṛgu, have arrived to see Hara, the best of the gods; / announce me quickly to the great-souled Śaṃkara."
Hearing that speech of his, Nandin, the lord of all the attendants, / spoke harsh words to the great sage of boundless splendor:
"Access to that lord is impossible; Śaṃkara is dallying with the goddess. / Turn back, O best of sages, if you wish to live."
Thus turned away by him, the great ascetic stayed there / for many days at that entrance to the house of the great lord.
[Bhṛgu thought:] "Since he, intoxicated by union with a woman, disdains me, / therefore his form shall indeed become a vulva and a phallus.
Overcome by darkness, he disrespects me, a brahmin; / fallen into unfriendliness toward brahmins, he is unworthy of worship by twice-born men.
Therefore, food, water, flowers, and likewise oblation offered to him, / all that shall become defiled remnants of worship; of this there is no doubt."
Having thus cursed Śaṃkara, who is worshiped by the world, the exceedingly radiant one / spoke to the extremely fierce attendant Nandin, holding a trident, O king:
"And whoever in the world are devotees of Rudra, bearing ashes, lingas, and bones, / let them indeed become heretics, excluded from the Vedas."
Having thus cursed Rudra, the destroyer of Tripura, the sage / went to Brahmā's world, which is bowed to by all the worlds.
Seeing Brahmā Parameṣṭhin seated there along with the gods, / the highly intelligent [sage] bowed to the god with folded hands.
Having bowed before him, the great ascetic remained silent; / seeing that tiger among sages, [Brahmā,] enveloped by the quality of rajas,
the Creator did not honor the great sage who had arrived; / neither standing up in greeting nor kind words were offered to him by the Ordainer.
The lotus-seated god remained there in such great sovereign arrogance; / seeing the lotus-seated one overcome by excess of rajas,
the exceedingly radiant [sage] spoke words to the grandfather of the worlds: / "Since, exceedingly overcome by rajas, you disdain me,
therefore attain unworthiness of worship among all the worlds." / Having thus cursed the great-souled Brahmā, who was worshiped by the world,
the brahmin Bhṛgu went at once to the temple of the Lord; / having entered the realm of Viṣṇu on the northern shore of the milk ocean,
